WARNING

RE:
CITATION:
Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. M.S.2, 2010 ONSC 3878

COURT FILE NO.:  FS-09-00016492

The
court hearing this matter directs that the following notice should be attached
to the file:

This is a case under Part III of the
Child and
Family Services Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.11 and is subject to one or
more of subsections 48(7), 45(8) and 45(9) of the Act.

These
subsections and
subsection 85(3)
of the
Child and Family Services Act,
which
deals with the consequences of failure to comply, read as follows:

45.-(7)
Order excluding media representatives or
prohibiting publication –

The court may make an order,

.  .  .

(c) prohibiting the publication of a report of the
hearing or a specified part of the hearing,

Where the court is of the opinion that … publication
of the report, …, would cause emotional harm to a child who is a witness at or
a participant in the hearing or is the subject of the proceeding.

(8)
Prohibition: identifying child. –
No
person shall publish or make public information that has the effect of
identifying a child who is a witness at or a participant in a hearing or the
subject or a proceeding, or the child’s parent or foster parent or a member of
the child’s family.

(9)
Idem: order re adult. –
The court may make
an order prohibiting the publication of information that has the effect of
identifying a person charged with an offence under this Part.

.  .  .

85. – (3)
Idem
– a person who contravenes
subsection 45(8) or 76(11) (publication of identifying information) or an order
prohibiting publication made under clause 45(7)(c) or subsection 45(9), and a
director, officer, or employee of a corporation who authorizes, permits or
concurs in such a contravention by the corporation, is guilty of an offence and
on conviction is liable to a fine of not more than $10,000 or to imprisonment
for a term of not more than three years, or to both.

HEARD:
June 28, 2010

Kelly
J.

REASONS FOR
DECISION

[
1
]

The two
children involved in this appeal are L.S. born May […], 2004 and T.S. born on
May […], 2006.  Their mother is Ms. M.S.2, the appellant.  Their father is Mr.
R.S. who did not participate in this appeal.

[
2
]

There are
three other children in the S. family.  C.S. (born on July […], 1996), M.S.1(born
on June […], 2004) and K.S. (born August […], 1993).  The decisions made by
Waldman J. regarding M.S.1and C.S. are not being appealed.  K.S. was not the
subject of the decision by Waldman J.

[
3
]

The
Society has had a lengthy history with this family commencing in 1993.  The
original protection application involving the four eldest children commenced in
2005.  They were found to be children in need of protection.  In January, 2006,
they were placed in the care and custody of their mother subject to the
supervision of the Society.

[
4
]

The
protection issues which gave rise to the Application in 2005 related to the
father’s mental health.  The terms of supervision required that the mother not
live with the father or allow him to have contact with the children until the
Society approved the contact.  The supervision ordered continued through 2006
and 2007.  The youngest child, T.S., was found to be in need of protection in
June, 2007.

[
5
]

On August
23, 2007, the children were apprehended by the Society as a result of
disclosures made by K.S. that the father was frequently in the family home in
violation of Society supervision orders.  L.S. and T.S. have been in foster
care since that time.  They have remained in care long past the statutory time
line set out under the
Child and Family Services Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c.
C.11 (“CFSA”).

[
6
]

The matter
proceeded before Waldman J. in the summer of 2009.  The issue in the case was
the risk of harm that the father presents to the children, given his untreated
mental illness and the ability of the mother to protect the children from their
father.

[
7
]

After a
six-day trial in the Ontario Court of Justice and after hearing from eleven
witnesses, Waldman J. made the two children who are the subject of this appeal
Crown Wards, with no access, for the purpose of adoption.  Their mother appeals
from that decision.

[
8
]

The mother
submits that the judge erred as follows:

(1)

making inferences of fact that were not supported by the evidence;

(2)

failing to consider the
CFSA
in making the Crown Wardship order; and

(3)

failing to order access to the two children.

[
9
]

The
Society and the Office of the Children’s Lawyer take the position that the
appeal should be dismissed.  I agree.

The Standard of Review

[
10
]

In coming to my conclusion that
the appeal should be dismissed, I have considered the principles regarding the
standard of review that were set out by the Supreme Court of Canada in the case
of
Housen v. Nikolaisen
,
2002 SCC 33 (CanLII)
, [2002] S.C.J. No. 31 at paras.
10 and 23
.  In
short, an appellate court may interfere with a trial judge’s findings only if
there has been a “palpable and overriding error” which constitutes a
substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.  A palpable error is one that is
plainly seen on the face of the record.

[
11
]

Factual findings made by a trial
judge are entitled to significant deference on appeal.  If there is an
indication that the trial judge did not consider relevant factors or evidence,
this may demonstrate that the trial judge did not consider the relevant factors
or evidence.  An omission is only a material error “if it gives rise to the
reasoned belief that the trial judge must have forgotten, ignored or
misconceived the evidence in a way that affected his conclusion”.  (See:
Van
de Perre v. Edwards
,
2001 SCC 60 (CanLII)
, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 1014 (S.C.C.).)

[
12
]

The decision of the trial judge,
particularly in matters of family law, should not be interfered with lightly by
appellate courts.  The trial judge is in the best position to decide the best
interests of the child.  (See:
C. (G.C.) v. New Brunswick (Minister of
Health and Community Services) [G.C.C.]
,
1988 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1988] S.C.J. No. 48 (S.C.C.) at
paragraph
5
and
New Brunswick (Minister of Health and Community Services) v.
M.L.
,
1998 CanLII 800 (SCC)
, [1998] S.C.J. No. 52 (S.C.C.) at paragraphs
34-35
.)

[
13
]

I will now apply the standard of
review to the grounds of appeal raised by the mother.

Ground
No. 1:        Did Waldman J. make findings that were not

supported
by the evidence?

[
14
]

The first ground of appeal
advanced by the mother is that the trial judge made findings that were not
supported by the evidence.  The trial judge found that:

(a)

the mother and the father are not separated and if they are, they will
not remain separated;

(b)

L.S. and T.S. would be exposed to the risk of physical and emotional
harm if they resided with their mother and that the mother is unable to make
her children’s needs and safety a priority; and

(c)

L.S. and T.S.’s needs would not be met if returned to the mother.

[
15
]

I find that the evidence before
Waldman J. to support the above-mentioned findings was overwhelming.  I will
deal with these three issues separately.

(a)

The Separation of the Mother and Father

[
16
]

The mother submits that she
presented evidence to show that she and the father were separated at the time
of trial and that they would remain separated.  She takes issue with the trial
judge’s reliance on the evidence of Dr. Nitza Perlman who performed a parenting
capacity assessment.  Dr. Perlman found that the mother continued to want the
reunification of the family and she saw this as a problematic choice.  The
trial judge accepted this evidence.

[
17
]

In my view, the evidence of Dr. Perlman
was but just one piece in the puzzle of the overwhelming evidence that either
the parties were not separated or they would not remain separated.

[
18
]

The mother testified that she was
permanently separated from the father at the time of the trial.  Initially she
said that they had been separated for two years.  Then she testified that she
maintained their relationship after separation and she was unable to give clear
dates as to when their relationship ended.  She claims that she had been
enlightened about the father’s illness as a result of counseling and as a
result, the parties would remain separated.

[
19
]

Despite the mother’s testimony,
there was ample evidence for the trial judge to find that she did not believe
that the relationship between the father and mother was permanently over.
There was a fifteen-year history of reconciliation despite the domestic
violence, criminal orders prohibiting contact and the family court orders
restricting access between the father and the children.

[
20
]

The evidence which supports the
trial judge’s findings may be summarized as follows:

Date

Occurrence

August, 1993

The Society
received a referral from the community but closed the file because the mother
refused to cooperate with the investigation.

January, 1997

The Society
received a referral from the Queen Street Mental Health Centre.  The father
had escaped from their secure unit and was assessed as violent and
dangerous.  There was a concern that he might try and contact his family.
The mother refused the services of the Society and no concerns were verified.

March 11, 2000

The police
found the mother, who was pregnant at the time, and two young children locked
in a small room with a padlock on the outside of the door, providing no
access to a bathroom or a kitchen.  At that time the mother informed the
police that the father had locked them inside when he left the apartment.
The mother later recanted her statement and the charges against the father
were dropped.

May 18, 2000

The Court
granted a temporary Supervision Order in response to a Protection Application
brought by the Society.

August 21, 2000

The children
(K.S. and C.S.) were apprehended after the Society received the father’s
mental health records.  The records disclosed that the father suffered from
bipolar disorder and that he had been hospitalized on a number of occasions
during manic phases which occurred every 12 to 18 months.  K.S. and C.S. were
placed with their maternal grandmother under a Supervision Order.  After the
children were placed with their grandmother, the father entered a manic phase
and at one point ended up in the hospital with two gunshot wounds.

July 16,
2001

K.S. and C.S. were returned to the father and the mother under a
Supervision Order and the Society eventually terminated their involvement on
December 21, 2001.

Fall of 2003

The Society
became re-involved with the family in the fall of 2003 when the school
contacted the Society to express concerns about K.S. and C.S.’s sporadic
attendance at school.  The Society was also contacted by the police to advise
that the father had been charged with assault and had been admitted to the
Queen Street Mental Health Centre.  As a result of his charges, the father
was subject to bail conditions prohibiting contact with the mother.

November, 2004

The Society
closed its file in November, 2004 as the Society believed that the family
situation was relatively calm and the mother reported that her husband was
doing well.

August 24, 2005

The Society
subsequently brought a Protection Application dated August 24, 2005 with
respect to K.S., Chantel, M.S.1and L.S..  The Application cited the ongoing
cycle of domestic violence, the father’s serious mental health condition, the
father’s frequent admissions to the hospital for violent episodes, the frequent
attendance of the police at their home for domestic incidents and the
mother’s inability to take the necessary steps to protect her children from
the father.

January 17, 2006

The children
were found to be in need of protection under ss. 37(2)(b) and (g) of the CFSA
and placed with the mother under a six-month Supervision Order with terms and
conditions, including a term that the mother was not to allow the father to
have any contact with the children unless approved by the Society.

2006-2007

The supervision
Orders were extended.

May 10, 2007

The father
was charged with assaulting the mother.  The assault was witnessed by a
neighbour and portions of the assault were recorded on video, including
screams from the children, some of whom were present during the assault.

May 18, 2007

The father
was arrested in the family home and he was found by the police cowering under
the beds in the children’s bedroom.

August 23, 2007

K.S.
disclosed that the father was frequently in the home and the children were
all afraid of him.  The children, including T.S. who was a year old, were all
apprehended.  At this time the father had a criminal bail condition
prohibiting contact with the mother and there was a condition in the
Supervision Order that the mother not allow the father in the home.  The
mother testified that K.S. made this disclosure to the Society because she
and K.S. were having a fight.

July 3, 2008

The father
was convicted of assaulting the mother.  At the trial, the mother denied the
assault and the presence of the children during the assault.  She testified
at the father’s criminal trial that the assault did not take place.  The
father was convicted on the basis of evidence from a neighbor and the
videotape of a portion of the assault.

Hryn J. made
the following finding when he convicted the father of assaulting his wife:

“The
accused’s wife [the mother] is more intent on lying to protect her husband
[the father] than to admit she recognized her own children’s screams of
terror, which are obvious to anyone who plays Exhibit number one [a partial
video of the assault].”

August,
2008

Dr. Perlman conducted a parenting capacity assessment of the mother.
Dr. Perlman concluded that the mother did not see the father as a danger to
herself or the children and did not believe that he presented a danger of
emotional or physical harm.  Dr. Perlman also concluded that there was no
evidence that the mother would end her relationship with the father for the
sake of having her children in her care.

October 8, 2008

The mother
requested that the conditions of the father’s probation be varied to remove
all conditions that restricted their contact.

October/November2008

The mother
attended a counseling session and discussed her decision to stay with the
father.  She did not show up for her next scheduled counseling appointment
and did not return phone calls to arrange a subsequent session.

June, 2009

M.S.1reported
that he had seen his father during an unsupervised outing with his mother on
Father’s Day.  L.S. and T.S. also reported seeing their father on this
occasion.  The mother takes the position that the children are mistaken and
that they saw a relative of the father whose appearance is similar to his.

July, 2009

The father
was arrested and he telephoned the mother on her cell phone to ask her to be
his surety for release.  The mother declined.

[
21
]

The trial judge weighed the
evidence, assessed the credibility of the mother and came to the conclusion
that the conduct of the mother did not support her testimony that she and the
father had separated in 2008 and would remain separated.  At paragraph 65 of
her Reasons for Judgment, the trial judge found that:

(a)

the mother testified at the father’s criminal trial in 2008 and denied
the assault;

(b)

the mother signed the document that probation required authorizing
contact and the explanation she offered was not reasonable;

(c)

the mother arranged for father to see the children on Father’s Day,
2009;

(d)

the mother was on a crusade to convince Dr. Perlman that the family,
including the father, should be reunited;

(e)

the mother continues to be very connected to and committed to the
father;

(f)

the mother did attend some counseling sessions which she ended
prematurely;

(g)

the mother’s actions in the past and, in particular, continuing to allow
the father to be with the children after the Society’s involvement support the
strong connection between mother and father;

(h)

the mother continues to minimize the father’s violence; and

(i)

the mother has not taken any other steps which would allow the court to
conclude that anything is likely to be different in the future regarding her
connection to the father.

[
22
]

In my view, the above-mentioned
findings of the trial judge should not be interfered with by the Appellate
Court.  There was evidence on the record that supports her findings.  As such,
there was no overriding or palpable error in coming to the conclusion that the
trial judge did regarding separation.   (See:
Housen v. Nikolaisen
,
supra

and
Waxman v. Waxman
,
2004 CanLII 39040 (ON CA)
, [2004] O.J. No. 1765 (C A.) at paras.
336-337
.)

(b)

That L.S. and T.S. would be exposed to the risk of physical and
emotional harm if they resided with their mother and that the mother is unable
to make her children’s needs and safety a priority.

[
23
]

The history of the proceedings set
out above aptly provide the evidence upon which Waldman J. was able to conclude
that L.S. and T.S. would be exposed to the risk of physical and emotional harm
if they resided with their mother.  It is clear that based upon the evidence
produced at trial, the mother is unable to make her children’s needs and safety
a priority.

[
24
]

The mother submits that since the
apprehension of L.S., T.S. and the other children, she has not resided with the
father.  She says that the father does not know where she lives and therefore
the children would not be at risk of emotional and/or physical harm if they
resided with her.

[
25
]

The mother also submits that she
has greater insight into the father’s mental illness and the impact that it has
had on the family as a result of counseling.  She has also gained insight into
the inappropriateness of the father’s violence towards her.  That is what makes
this current separation different and of lasting permanence that will reduce
the risk of physical and emotional harm if they reside with their mother.

[
26
]

The mother also testified that she
has the emotional and financial support of her family who could provide shelter
for her in the case of emergency.  She would call 9-1-1 right away if any
problems arose regarding the father.  She submits that the evidence that L.S.
and T.S. would be at risk of physical harm if they reside with her is purely
speculative.

[
27
]

The trial judge considered the
mother’s evidence and found that notwithstanding the involvement of the
Society, the police and the imposition of court orders (both in the family
court and in the criminal court) these parties cannot stay away from each other.
No amount of adversity could keep the mother from seeing the father which puts
the children at risk.  Such is the case despite the plan advanced by the mother
to protect the children.

[
28
]

In
Jewish Family and Child
Service of Toronto v. R.K.
, Sherr J. described the impact of domestic
violence and chaos on children even when the parent has good parenting skills
in other areas:

Neither R. nor T. could understand the society’s concerns at
trial and felt that the apprehension was entirely unwarranted.  They argued
that K [the child] was never harmed and that they cared for him in a proper and
loving fashion.
In fact, the evidence led at this trial was that, for a
parent of her age, R’s instrumental parenting skills are very good.
She is
able to properly feed, clothe and bathe K.  She interacts very well with him.  R.
loves K. and would never intentionally hurt him.
However, having good
parenting skills does not always equate with being a competent parent.  A
competent parent must be able to make sound choices to keep their child safe.
He or she must be able to protect a child from chaos and conflict.  Children,
even infants, who are continually exposed to conflict, are at a high risk of
emotional harm and impaired development.
[Emphasis added]

(See:
Jewish Family and Child Service of Toronto v.
R.K.
,
2008 ONCJ 774 (CanLII)
, [2008] O.J. No. 5856 (O.C.J.) at para.
57
(affirmed by the Court of
Appeal at
2009 ONCA 903 (CanLII)
, [2009], O.J. No. 5422).)

[
29
]

The above-mentioned passage from
Sherr J. is directly applicable to this case.  It was agreed by all parties
that the mother has strengths as a parent.  The trial judge found the mother
was able to meet the children’s instrumental needs and she was described as
“child focused”.  (See:  Reasons for Judgment, para. 35.)  However, these
strengths have to be balanced against her inability to protect L.S. and T.S.
from the chaos that has had a pervasive presence in the family as a result of
the father’s mental health issues.

[
30
]

There was extensive evidence, as
highlighted above, to support the contention that the children were at risk of
emotional harm and that their mother could not meet their needs.  The trial
judge found that the mother had shown little insight into the impact of the father’s
mental health on the children.  The mother would remove the children from the
house when the father became agitated.  She testified that the children thought
that his rapid speech was funny.  The children were present when the father assaulted
the mother and when the police came into their home and found father hiding
under their beds.  The children were involved when they had to escape from the
apartment when the father came through the window.  They were forced to hide in
the car.  The children were also involved when they had to leave their own home
and stay at their grandmother’s because of the father’s behavior.

[
31
]

The mother also testified that
because of the father’s behavior, the children missed school and that they had
to move a lot.  The mother acknowledged that managing the father’s illness
requires a lot of energy.  She is not always able to meet the children’s needs
as a result of the father’s illness.

[
32
]

As a result of these factual
findings, Waldman J. concluded that the children had been exposed to a
significant amount of violence and erratic behavior by their father.  This is
worsened because of the mother’s need to focus on the father’s emotional state which
detracts from her ability to meet the children’s needs.  Waldman J. rightly concluded
that the father’s presence in the home represents a serious risk of harm to the
children.

[
33
]

The mother had fifteen years worth
of opportunities and second chances to recognize the dangers presented to her
children by continuing a relationship with the father.  She chose not to take
the steps that would have saved the children from having to be placed in the
care of the Society.

[
34
]

The mother must stop experimenting
with her children’s lives.  There has to be some demonstrated basis for a
determination that the mother is able to parent the children without
unreasonably endangering the children’s safety.  The mother failed to do so at
the trial before Waldman J.  (See:
Jewish Child and Family Services v. R.K.
,

supra
, at para. 68.)

[
35
]

Applying the decision in
Waxman
v. Waxman
,
supra
, there is evidence to support the findings that the
children were at risk of emotional harm and that the children’s needs would not
be met in their mother’s care.  This ground of appeal must also fail, as the
findings of fact and the inferences were supported by the evidence.

(c)

L.S. and T.S.’s Needs would not be Met by the Mother

[
36
]

Having found that the mother was
not separated from the father and/or would not stay separated from him, the
trial judge found that L.S. and Trish’s needs would not be met if returned to
the mother.

[
37
]

The trial judge noted that T.S.
had been referred to a psychiatrist and to Kinark Family Services and found
that she is a vulnerable child.  The trial judge also found that L.S. took a
period of time to adjust in the foster home to overcome her fear of men.

[
38
]

The mother submits that there was
evidence at the trial that she had experience with children with special needs
and that she was able to address those needs.  The mother also testified that
if the children were returned to her care, she would enroll them in programs to
ensure that their needs were met.

[
39
]

The mother takes the position that
she clearly demonstrated that she would be willing to work with the Society to
meet the children’s needs.  Waldman J. recognized this and referred to it in
her judgment at paragraph 24.

[
40
]

The mother’s willingness to
cooperate with the Society is repeated in her affidavit sworn on June 24, 2010
and submitted before this Court as fresh evidence.  The mother swears that she
is “willing to do everything and anything required to demonstrate to the Court
and the Society that she is a protective, caring and loving mother”.  I do not
accept the mother’s submission in this regard.

[
41
]

In my view, the evidence of the
mother that she would be able to address the needs of the children and work
with the Society was not borne out by the evidence at trial or the fresh
evidence filed before me.

[
42
]

There was ample evidence before
the court that indicates, in the past, the mother spent much energy and focus
on the father to the detriment of the children (and as outlined above).  The
fresh evidence filed on this appeal also supports Waldman J.’s conclusion that
the children’s needs would not be met if returned to the mother.  The mother is
already in breach of the Order of the trial judge.

[
43
]

At the conclusion of her judgment,
Waldman J. ordered, amongst other things, that:

(a)

the mother shall cooperate with the Society;

(b)

the mother shall allow scheduled and unscheduled visits by the Society
worker and shall allow the worker to meet in private with C.S. at home and at
school;

(c)

the mother shall notify the Society in advance of any change in address
and telephone number or family constellation.

[
44
]

The affidavit of Sarah Singer, a
Child Protection worker, was filed before the Court on consent.  It shows that
the mother has breached the Order of Waldman J. and she has not cooperated with
the Society.  Her evidence may be summarized as follows:

Date

Occurrence

January 4, 2010

Ms. Singer
attempted to contact the mother via the telephone number she had for her but
the telephone number was not in service.

January 5, 2010

Ms. Singer
met with the maternal grandmother and requested that she inform the mother
that Ms. Singer was trying to contact her but could not do so because her telephone
number was out of service.

January 7, 2010

A registered
letter was sent to the mother asking her to contact Ms. Singer.

January 14, 2010

A registered
letter was sent to the mother asking her to contact Ms. Singer.

January 20, 2010

Ms. Singer attended at the home of the mother with her
supervisor, Mr. Franz Noritz for an unscheduled visit. She heard male
and female voices from inside the apartment, along with the sound of running
water. Ms. Singer made several attempts of knocking loudly at the door and
calling out for the people in the apartment to open the door. No one opened
the door or responded. Ms. Singer left a note under the door requesting that
the mother contact her
.

January 27, 2010

Ms. Singer
obtained a new telephone number for the mother during C.S.’s school visit.
She called the number and left a message.

February 9, 2010

Ms. Singer
received a call from the mother.  The mother demanded to know how Ms. Singer
had obtained her telephone number.  A discussion ensued about the attempts
the Society had made to contact the mother.  A date and time was arranged to
meet the mother.
Ms. Singer attended at the
home and met with the mother. The mother indicated to her that C.S. was doing
well and that they did not need Society involvement.

February 16, 2010

Ms. Singer spoke with the mother regarding
the psychological report recently completed by Dr. Fitzgerald and generally
discussed his recommendations for C.S.. Ms. Singer offered to arrange a
meeting with Dr. Fitzgerald for the mother regarding his findings, and the
mother indicated that this was not necessary, as she felt that C.S. just
needed to try harder at school.  During this meeting, Ms. Singer also spoke
with the mother about meeting once per month at a mutually agreed time in order
to review how things were going.

February 19, 2010

Ms. Singer
spoke with the mother.

February 24 and 25, 2010

Ms. Singer
initiated calls to the mother but she was unable to leave a message as there
was no voicemail available.

February 25, 2010

Ms. Singer
spoke with the grandmother and asked her to pass a message on to the mother
because she was trying to serve her with court papers.

March 9,
2010

Ms. Singer called the mother but was unable to leave a message as
there was no voicemail option available.

March 11, 2010

Ms. Singer
called the mother but was unable to leave a message as there was no voicemail
option available.

March 15, 2010

Ms. Singer sent a registered letter (dated March 11,
2010) to the mother at her home. This letter was returned to the Society
office by Canada Post after it was not picked up at the local postal station.
Ms. Singer sent the same letter via regular postal service as well.

March 16, 2010

Ms. Singer left a voicemail message for the mother asking
that she contact her.

March 23, 2010

Ms. Singer left a voicemail message for the mother asking
that she contact her.

April 8, 2010

Ms. Singer called the mother but was unable to leave a
message.

April 13, 2010

Ms. Singer called the mother but was unable to leave a
message.

April 14, 2010

Ms. Singer sent a registered letter to the mother at her
home. This letter was returned to the Society office by Canada Post after it
was not picked up at the local postal station.

April 19, 2010

Ms. Singer attended at the mother’s residence for an
unannounced home visit. She was able to gain entry to the apartment building
complex and attended at the door of the mother’s apartment. She knocked but
there was no answer. Ms. Singer had brought along a copy of her March 11,
2010 letter and her April 13, 2010 letter, in a sealed envelope addressed to
the mother and slid the envelope underneath the apartment door.  As of the
date of swearing the affidavit, Ms. Singer had not since received any
response from the mother with respect to her attempts to contact her.

[
45
]

In response to the issues raised
in Ms. Singer’s affidavit, the mother provided an affidavit to the Court as
fresh evidence. The mother says that if she was at home when Ms. Singer
knocked, she would have answered.  To address the issue of hearing voices in
the apartment when Ms. Singer attended, she swore that the television may have
been the source of the female and male voices that Ms. Singer heard because she
leaves the television on when she vacates the home for security purposes.  The
sound of running water may have been the washing machine.

[
46
]

The mother denies receiving the
notes that Ms. Singer left under the door.  However, there is no response to
Ms. Singer’s evidence regarding the registered mail sent, the telephone
messages left and the messages given to the maternal grandmother for the mother
to contact the Society.  Despite this, she claims that she has been in
compliance with Waldman J.’s order and is willing to work with the
Society.  I do not accept her evidence in this regard.

[
47
]

If the mother was really
interested in demonstrating that she is willing to do everything and anything
to show that she is a protective, caring and loving mother and had complied
with Waldman J.’s order then why did the Society worker have to obtain her
telephone number from C.S.’s school?  Why didn’t she notify the Society in
advance of the change of her telephone number as required by the Order of
Waldman J.?  Why was Ms. Singer confronted with the question of how she
got the mother’s telephone number when she received the first telephone call
from the Society?

[
48
]

Why was the mother not willing to
meet with Dr. Fitzgerald who authored a psychological report for C.S.?  Why
were the telephone messages and letters from the Society unanswered?  Lastly,
why didn’t the mother contact the Society to remain in contact with them once
per month as requested by Ms. Singer?

[
49
]

The answer to all of these
questions is simple. Waldman J. correctly found that L.S. and Trish’s needs
would not be met if returned to the mother.  As such, no error exists that
would call into question the conclusion of the trial judge.  This ground of
appeal must also fail.

Ground No. 2:  Did the Trial Judge Err in Not
Giving Full Consideration to the
CFSA
?

[
50
]

Pursuant to
s. 57(3)
of the
CFSA
,
the trial judge must choose the least disruptive alternative that will protect
a child. The alternative must be in the best interests of the child pursuant to

Section 37(3)
of the CFSA which provides:

37 (3)    Where a person is directed in this Part to make an
order or determination in the best interests of a child, the person shall take
into consideration those of the following circumstances of the case that he or
she considers relevant:

1.      The child’s physical,
mental and emotional needs, and the appropriate care or treatment to meet those
needs.

2.      The child’s physical,
mental and emotional level of development.

3.      The child’s cultural
background.

4.      The religious faith, if
any, in which the child is being raised.

5.      The importance for the
child’s development of a positive relationship with a parent and a secure place
as a member of a family.

6.      The child’s relationships
and emotional ties to a parent, sibling, relative, other member of the child’s
extended family or member of the child’s community.

7.      The importance of
continuity in the child’s care and the possible effect on the child of
disruption of that continuity.

8.      The merits of a plan for
the child’s care proposed by a society, including a proposal that the child be
placed for adoption or adopted, compared with the merits of the child remaining
with or returning to a parent.

9.      The child’s views and
wishes, if they can be reasonably ascertained.

10.    The effects on the child of
delay in the disposition of the case.

11.      The risk that the child
may suffer harm through being removed from, kept away from, returned to or
allowed to remain in the care of a parent.

12.      The degree of risk, if
any, that justified the finding that the child is in need of protection.

13.      Any other relevant
circumstance.

[
51
]

The mother takes the position that
the trial judge erred in not ordering a less disruptive alternative than making
the children Crown Wards with no access.  She submits that Waldman J. did not
give the appropriate weight to her ability to meet L.S. and T.S.’s needs nor the
harm in severing their relationships with their mother and their siblings.  I
disagree.

[
52
]

In lengthy, careful and
comprehensive reasons, the trial judge articulated the law that governs the
type of orders that are available to the court. Waldman J. took specific note
in paragraph 8 of her decision about the Society’s attempts to work with the
mother to reach a conclusion that was less disruptive than the result.  She
accepts that the Society did try to work with the mother for many years outside
of the court process.  When the Society did bring the matter to court, they
worked with the mother under a number of supervision orders before they took
the step of apprehending the children.  Waldman J. found that the Society
consistently tried to work with the mother because she was observed to have
strengths and it was hoped that the mother and children could be kept
together.  Despite these efforts, the trial judge found that the mother has
been very committed to the father and believes that she is unable to protect
the children.  (See:  Reasons for Judgment, para. 8.)

[
53
]

Waldman J. also explained, in
great detail, the factors she considered to determine the dispositions for L.S.
and T.S..  She referred to the fact that L.S. and T.S. had been in care for the
majority of their lives and the fact that they were unable to offer any self
protection due to their age.  Waldman J. referred to the fact that the children
had both done well in care and that they were eminently adoptable at three and
five years of age (at the time of trial).  (See:  Reasons for Judgment, paras.
27-31 and 43-48.)

[
54
]

Waldman J. correctly identified
and considered the test applicable to the dispositional determination that the
court was required to make.  She focused on the best interests of the children
in making her order.  The evidentiary record and the reasons for judgment
demonstrate that no error exists that would call into question the conclusion
of the trial judge.

Ground No. 3:  Did the Trial Judge Err in not
Ordering Access?

[
55
]

The mother submits that Waldman J.
erred in making an order of Crown Wardship, with no access to L.S. and T.S..
The mother also argues that Waldman J. erred in severing the relationship
between L.S. and T.S. and their older siblings.  I do not agree.

(a)

No Access to the Mother

[
56
]

The trial Judge was required to
apply the access test that existed prior to the 2006 amendments to the
CFSA
as
the Protection Application in this case was originally brought in 2005.  Under
the transition provisions to the 2006 amendments, all applications brought
prior to the amendments must be dealt with under s. 59(2), rather than s.
59(2.1).  (See:  S. 59(2), CFSA and
Ontario Regulation 495/06, s. 2
.)

[
57
]

Section 59(2)
of the
CFSA
provides
that if an order for Crown Wardship is determined to be in the best interests
of a child, there is a presumption that there will be no access to the
parents.  The court is prohibited from making an order for access to a person
unless it is satisfied that the relationship between the person and the child
is beneficial and meaningful to the child and, the ordered access will not
impair the child’s future opportunities for a permanent or stable placement.

[
58
]

The presumption against access
supports the overall statutory scheme for permanence through adoption. Once the
maximum length of time for temporary wardship has run out, if a child cannot be
safely returned home, a Crown Wardship order is the only remaining option. A
Society has a duty to make all reasonable efforts to assist a Crown ward to
develop a positive, secure and enduring relationship within a family through
either adoption, a custody order under s. 65.2(1) or customary care.  (See:

CFSA, s.70(1)
,
s. 63.1
.)

[
59
]

A child cannot be placed for
adoption until any access orders have been terminated.  (See:
CFSA, s. 141.1
.)

[
60
]

Although there was evidence that L.S.
and T.S. were bonded to their mother and older siblings, the evidence was that L.S.
and T.S. were adoptable by three available adoptive families that were a match
for them.  An order for access would have impaired L.S. and T.S.’s future
opportunities for a permanent and stable environment.

[
61
]

The parents were unable to
discharge the reverse onus against access.  They were unable to show that the
children could have a permanent and stable placement even if an access order was
made.  There was no palpable and overriding error in the trial judge’s finding
that the children were adoptable and the trial judge correctly applied the law
denying access to the mother.

(b)

No Access to the Siblings

[
62
]

The issue of sibling access
requires a different analysis than access to the mother.  A number of courts
have accepted the argument that a sibling access order, made as an order of
access from the younger children to the older children, will not impede
adoption and not attract the prohibition under
s. 141.1
of the
CFSA
.  Therefore,
if the access is beneficial and meaningful there is a possibility of overcoming
the second prohibition in
s. 59(2)
by taking the position that the access order
would not legally impair the child’s ability to be placed for adoption.  In
this particular case, neither the Society nor the Office of the Children’s
Lawyer advances a sibling access argument.  (See:
Re A.G.
,
[2009] O.J.
No. 2875 (S.C.J.) at paras. 5-6
.)

[
63
]

The two children who are the
subject of this appeal were represented by counsel in this trial (Mr. Herb
Stover).  Mr. Stover did not request an order for inter sibling access between L.S.
and T.S. and the older siblings nor did the mother.

[
64
]

While a sibling access order would
not necessarily impede adoption, in these particular circumstances there was no
request before the Court for access between the older siblings and the younger
siblings who are the subject of this appeal.  In the absence of this request,
there was no case presented to discharge the presumption against access under

s. 59(2)
.

[
65
]

There was no error, on the facts
of this particular case, in failing to allow for sibling access between L.S.
and T.S. and their older siblings.

Dispostion

[
66
]

For the
abovementioned reasons, the appeal is dismissed.
